canonicalExplanation.summary: Smart pointers state **who owns** a heap object. **`std::unique_ptr<T>`** is the default: **exactly one owner**, no overhead, deletes the object automatically, and ownership can be **moved** but not copied. **`std::shared_ptr<T>`** means **shared ownership**: a reference count deletes the object when the last owner goes away, which costs extra and makes lifetimes harder to reason about, so use it only when ownership is **genuinely shared**. **`std::weak_ptr<T>`** observes a shared object **without owning** it (and breaks reference cycles). For code that just **uses** an object without owning it, pass a plain `T&` or `T*`. Create them with `std::make_unique` and `std::make_shared`; never write `delete`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner makes every pointer a shared_ptr "to be safe". Two objects end up holding shared_ptrs to each other, so neither is ever freed, and nobody can tell who's responsible for anything. A factory returns unique_ptr<Widget>, transferring exclusive ownership to the caller without an explicit delete. In this lesson you'll choose and justify an ownership representation without unnecessary shared ownership.

examples.title: A factory that hands over a Widget
examples.situation: A factory returns unique_ptr<Widget>, transferring exclusive ownership to the caller without an explicit delete.
walkthrough: **A factory returns unique_ptr<Widget>:** make_widget uses std::make_unique to build the widget.
**Transferring exclusive ownership to the caller:** w owns the widget; panel.push_back(std::move(w)) moves it on.
**Without an explicit delete:** the widget will be freed when panel is destroyed.
examples.result: Ownership is visible in every signature, and nothing leaks.

examples.title: The parent and child cycle
examples.situation: A Parent holds shared_ptr<Child> and each Child holds shared_ptr<Parent>. Memory is never freed.
walkthrough: The two shared_ptrs keep each other's counts at 1 or more.
The parent owns its children: keep shared_ptr (or unique_ptr) there.
Children only refer back: use weak_ptr<Parent> or a raw Parent* that doesn't own.
examples.result: Destroying the parent frees the whole tree.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: shared_ptr is the safest default for every pointer because more owners always prevent lifetime bugs.
misconceptions.correction: Shared ownership blurs responsibility, adds cost, and can create cycles that never free. Use unique_ptr unless ownership is genuinely shared.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why were the two objects never freed?

analogy.example: unique_ptr is **a car with one registered owner**: you can sell it (move) but not duplicate the registration. shared_ptr is **a timeshare**: the property stays until the last co-owner leaves. weak_ptr is **a friend with the address**: they can visit if it still exists, but they don't keep it standing.
limitations: Timeshares have fees; shared_ptr has counting overhead.
Two timeshares owning each other never close.

remediation.explanation: For every pointer ask: **does this code own the object, share it, or just use it?** Own: unique_ptr. Share (really): shared_ptr. Use: reference or raw pointer.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The parent and child cycle".

recap.summary: To choose ownership representations, default to unique_ptr for exclusive ownership (moved, never copied), use shared_ptr only when lifetime is genuinely shared, observe shared objects with weak_ptr to avoid cycles, pass plain references to functions that only use an object, and create with make_unique and make_shared.
